newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany says Communist states shared Vatican spies.
newsitem.headline: Germany says Communist states shared Vatican spies.

text.p: Eastern European spy agencies received detailed information from deep in the Vatican detailing conversations between the Pope and Western leaders during the Cold War, a German government office said on Monday.

The Gauck authority that has been examining millions of documents left behind by the defunct East German security police, or Stasi, said East Bloc agencies had spied on the Vatican between 1963 and 1988.
Johannes Legner, a spokesman for the Berlin-based Gauck authority, said many East Bloc agencies kept a close watch on the Vatican and shared their intelligence with each other.

"We have found a series of documents (in the Stasi files) that refer to high-level meetings between the Pope and Western leaders," Legner told Reuters. "Many of them were originally obtained by the Polish secret service."
The Vatican had no immediate comment.

The Berlin daily Der Tagesspiegel reported on Gauck agency documents two weeks ago that suggested Poland's SB secret service had a mole in the Vatican, possibly a top Polish cleric in the Roman Catholic Church administration.

Legner said 300 pages of new Stasi material had been found recently, including details of converations between Pope Paul VI and U.S. Transportation Secretary John Volpe and other senior Western government officials.
Many of the documents were translated from Italian into Polish and then Russian before being translated into German.
He said the Polish secret service in particular seem to have the most extensive sources within the vatican.
"The East German security police had sources as well, but apparently not at the same high levels as the Poles and Hungarians," Legner said.
Fearful of a possible uprising by its own overwhelmingly Catholic population, Poland was especially concerned about what was going on inside the walls of the Vatican, Legner said.
Even though there were few Catholics in communist East Germany, Legner said the Stasi was still interested in the Pope, especially because of his contacts with Western leaders.
The reports were addressed to spymaster Markus Wolf, the head of the Stasi's foreign intelligence section.
"Everything was interesting for the Stasi," said Legner.

In one file obtained by Reuters, marked "Top Secret" and "Translated from Russian" and dated July 4, 1970, the Pope and U.S. diplomat Henry Cabot Lodge are quoted discussing at length the Vietnam War, the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, and Cold War political tensions.
Lodge, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam, was one of President Richard Nixon's special envoys to the Paris peace talks with Hanoi.

"We were absolutely forced to undertake these efforts in order to quickly end the war," Lodge replied when the Pope admonished Lodge that the American bombing of Cambodia had made the Vietnam war more complicated.
"Our soldiers have already left Cambodia," he assured the Pope. "We have only left behind a few of our casulties."
Lodge told the Pope that the 1970 attacks on Cambodia had "weakened the communists" and that many weapons had been captured.
"I am convinced that we have created the groundwork for constructive negotiations for peace," Lodge said.
